steps.decision: On its own line, before the matrix is touched. It earns the first mark, and it tells you straight away whether an inverse exists at all.

steps.working: Swap the leading diagonal and negate the other one: $\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
steps.decision: Two separate actions, done in that order. The leading diagonal moves and keeps its signs; the other diagonal stays put and changes sign. This line earns nothing on its own: the second mark is for the finished inverse, after the division.

options: Because swapping and negating is what makes the product come out as the identity
Because every entry of an inverse is the reciprocal of the original entry
Because the two diagonals are always interchangeable
whyMenu.explain: The arrangement is chosen precisely so that multiplying back gives the identity. Taking reciprocals entry by entry would not undo the matrix at all.

steps.working: Divide every entry by the determinant: $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{pmatrix}$.
steps.decision: Keep the $\frac{1}{5}$ outside the brackets or share it through all four entries, but do not do half of each. A determinant with a minus sign keeps it here.
It earns no mark of its own. It takes twenty seconds on a calculator paper, and it catches every sign slip in the three actions above.

steps.decision: The leading diagonal holds two negatives, so write each product out rather than doing it in your head: $(-3)(-1)$ is $3$, not $-3$. The determinant is negative, and that sign has to survive.
Negating an entry that is already negative makes it positive. Write each one down rather than trusting the pattern. This line earns nothing on its own: the second mark is for the finished inverse.

steps.working: Divide by $-5$, with brackets round it: $N^{-1} = \frac{1}{-5}\begin{pmatrix}-1 & -2 \\ -4 & -3\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\frac{1}{5} & \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{4}{5} & \frac{3}{5}\end{pmatrix}$.
steps.decision: This is the step the reports name. Writing $\frac{1}{5}$ instead would give $\begin{pmatrix}-\frac{1}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} \\ -\frac{4}{5} & -\frac{3}{5}\end{pmatrix}$, with every sign wrong.

Because the minus signs in the matrix cancel it out
whyMenu.explain: The determinant is $-5$, so the factor is $\frac{1}{-5}$. Dropping its sign changes all four entries.

items.stem:
Three quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new method, so answer from what you already know.
What is $(-3) \times (-1)$?

options.feedback: Two negatives multiply to a positive.
The two minus signs cancel, so the product is positive.
That is the sum. The determinant multiplies along each diagonal.

items.stem: What is $\frac{1}{4}$ of $-3$, written as a decimal?
items.skill: Dividing a negative by a whole number

options.feedback: Dividing a negative number leaves it negative.
The sign is unchanged by dividing, so the answer stays negative.
That is $-4$ divided by $3$. Here it is $-3$ divided by $4$.

items.stem: Which matrix is the identity for two by two multiplication?

options.feedback: Ones on the leading diagonal, zeros elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing.
Every entry is one, which is not the identity: multiplying by it changes the matrix.
That is the zero matrix. It sends everything to zero.
That is bc − ad, the subtraction taken the other way round.
That adds the two products. The determinant subtracts them: $15 - 8 = 7$.

items.stem: A matrix has determinant $0$. What follows?

options.text: It has no inverse, and it is called singular
options.feedback: The formula divides by the determinant, so there is nothing to divide by.

options.text: Its inverse is the zero matrix
options.feedback: No matrix at all multiplies it to give the identity, so there is no inverse to name.
The identity is its own inverse. A singular matrix has none.

items.stem: Which is the inverse of $\begin{pmatrix}5 & 1 \\ 4 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, whose determinant is 1?

options.feedback: 5 and 1 swap on the leading diagonal, 1 and 4 change sign, and dividing by 1 changes nothing.
The signs changed but the leading diagonal never swapped.
The leading diagonal swapped, but the other diagonal kept its signs.

items.stem: A matrix has determinant $-5$. What factor goes in front of the swapped and negated matrix?
items.skill: Keeping the sign of a negative determinant

options.feedback: The reciprocal of a negative number is negative, and the brackets keep it that way.
The minus sign has been dropped. That single slip changes all four entries, and the reports name it directly.
The determinant multiplies rather than divides here. The factor is its reciprocal.

items.stem: How do you check that a matrix you have written down really is the inverse?

options.text: Multiply it by the original matrix and look for the identity
options.feedback: That is the definition of an inverse, and it catches sign slips in seconds.

options.text: Add it to the original matrix and look for the zero matrix
options.feedback: An inverse undoes a multiplication, not an addition.

options.text: Check that every entry is the reciprocal of the original entry
options.feedback: An inverse is not built entry by entry; the whole matrix works together.
$ad - bc$, with the leading diagonal first.
That is $bc - ad$, taken the other way round.
That is $ad + bc$, with the two products added. The determinant subtracts them: $8 - 3 = 5$.

items.stem: Which of these is $A^{-1}$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{pmatrix}$, where $\det A = 5$?

options.feedback: Swapped, negated and then divided by $5$.
Swapped and negated, and then never divided by the determinant.
The signs changed but the leading diagonal never swapped.
Only the first entry was divided by the determinant; the other three were left as they were.

context.setting: A singular matrix, recognised from its determinant

parts.stem:
The matrix $S = \begin{pmatrix}3 & 6 \\ 2 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
Identify the correct statement about $S$.

options.feedback: The inverse formula divides by the determinant, and nothing divides by zero. A matrix like this is called singular.

options.text: $\det S = 0$, so $S^{-1}$ is the zero matrix
options.feedback: There is no inverse at all, not an inverse made of zeros. Nothing multiplies $S$ to give the identity.
The two diagonal products have been added. The determinant subtracts them: $12 - 12 = 0$, so $S$ has no inverse.

parts.workedSolution:
$\det S = (3)(4) - (6)(2) = 12 - 12 = 0$.
The inverse formula divides by the determinant, so $S$ has no inverse: $S$ is singular.

questions.solutionProgram: main: $\det S = (3)(4) - (6)(2) = 12 - 12 = 0$. The inverse formula divides by the determinant, so $S$ has no inverse: $S$ is singular.

context.setting: An inverse whose determinant is one, so the three actions stand alone

parts.stem:
The matrix $G = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 4 \\ 2 & 9\end{pmatrix}$.
Find $G^{-1}$.
Write the answer as a matrix. A fraction, a decimal or a fraction in front of the brackets is accepted.
hints: Swap the leading diagonal, negate the other one.
parts.workedSolution:
$\det G = (1)(9) - (4)(2) = 1$.
Swapping and negating gives $\begin{pmatrix}9 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, and dividing by $1$ leaves it unchanged.
So $G^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}9 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, and $G^{-1}G$ gives the identity.

commonErrors.feedback: The signs on the other diagonal changed, and the leading diagonal never swapped. With $a$ and $d$ exchanged as well, the inverse is $\begin{pmatrix}9 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.
The leading diagonal swapped, and $b$ and $c$ kept their signs. The other diagonal changes sign, which gives $\begin{pmatrix}9 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.solutionProgram: main: $\det G = (1)(9) - (4)(2) = 1$. Swapping and negating gives $\begin{pmatrix}9 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, and dividing by $1$ leaves it unchanged. So $G^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}9 & -4 \\ -2 & 1\end{pmatrix}$, and $G^{-1}G$ gives the identity.

parts.stem:
The matrix $A = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 2\end{pmatrix}$.
Find $A^{-1}$.
Write the answer as a matrix. A fraction, a decimal or a fraction in front of the brackets is accepted.
hints: Determinant on its own line first.
Swap, negate, then divide every entry.
parts.workedSolution:
$\det A = 5$.
Swapping and negating gives $\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$.
Dividing every entry by $5$:
$$A^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{pmatrix}$$

commonErrors.feedback: Swapped and negated correctly, and then handed in without the division. Every entry still has to be divided by $5$, which gives $\begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{pmatrix}$.
Only the first entry was divided by the determinant. The factor of $\frac{1}{5}$ reaches all four, giving $\begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{pmatrix}$.
The signs changed but the leading diagonal never swapped. With $a$ and $d$ exchanged the inverse is $\begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{pmatrix}$.
The leading diagonal swapped and the other diagonal kept its signs. Negating $b$ and $c$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{pmatrix}$.

questions.solutionProgram: main: $\det A = 5$. Swapping and negating gives $\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix}$. Dividing every entry by $5$: $A^{-1} = \frac{1}{5}\begin{pmatrix}2 & -1 \\ -3 & 4\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{5} & -\frac{1}{5} \\ -\frac{3}{5} & \frac{4}{5}\end{pmatrix}$.

Dividing by $\det A = 5$ gives $-1/5$.

commonErrors.feedback: The sign was changed but the entry was never divided by the determinant. Dividing $-1$ by $5$ gives $-1/5$.
The entry was divided by the determinant but never negated. The other diagonal changes sign, so the answer is $-1/5$.

context.setting: The value that makes a matrix singular, which is the determinant read as an equation

parts.stem:
The matrix $M = \begin{pmatrix}k & 4 \\ 3 & 6\end{pmatrix}$ has no inverse.
Find the value of $k$.
hints: A matrix has no inverse exactly when its determinant is zero.
Write the determinant in terms of $k$ and set it to zero.
parts.workedSolution:
$\det M = 6k - (4)(3) = 6k - 12$.
There is no inverse when the determinant is zero, so $6k - 12 = 0$.
Therefore $k = 2$.

commonErrors.feedback: Setting the determinant to zero is right, but $6k + 12$ adds the two diagonal products. The determinant subtracts them: $ad - bc = 6k - 12$, and $6k - 12 = 0$ gives $k = 2$.

questions.solutionProgram: main: $\det M = 6k - (4)(3) = 6k - 12$. There is no inverse when the determinant is zero, so $6k - 12 = 0$. Therefore $k = 2$.

parts.stem:
The matrix $F = \begin{pmatrix}7 & 3 \\ 4 & 2\end{pmatrix}$.
Find $F^{-1}$.
Write the answer as a matrix. A fraction, a decimal or a fraction in front of the brackets is accepted.
hints: Determinant on its own line first.
parts.workedSolution:
$\det F = (7)(2) - (3)(4) = 2$.
Swapping and negating gives $\begin{pmatrix}2 & -3 \\ -4 & 7\end{pmatrix}$.
Dividing by $2$:
$$F^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -2 & \frac{7}{2}\end{pmatrix}$$

commonErrors.feedback: Swapped and negated correctly, and then not divided by the determinant. Dividing every entry by $2$ gives $\begin{pmatrix}1 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -2 & \frac{7}{2}\end{pmatrix}$.
The leading diagonal swapped and $b$ and $c$ kept their signs. The other diagonal changes sign, giving $\begin{pmatrix}1 & -\frac{3}{2} \\ -2 & \frac{7}{2}\end{pmatrix}$.

parts.stem:
Write down the matrix $F^{-1}F$.
Write the answer as a matrix. A fraction, a decimal or a fraction in front of the brackets is accepted.
hints: An inverse undoes the matrix it came from.
parts.workedSolution:
An inverse multiplied by its own matrix gives the identity, so $F^{-1}F = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{pmatrix}$.
Multiplying it out is also a check on part (a).

The matrix $H = \begin{pmatrix}6 & 9 \\ 2 & 3\end{pmatrix}$.
Explain why $H$ has no inverse.

accepted: det H = 0, so H has no inverse because the formula divides by the determinant
the determinant of H is zero, so H is singular and has no inverse

hints: Name the matrix as well as the reason.
parts.workedSolution:
$\det H = (6)(3) - (9)(2) = 18 - 18 = 0$.
The determinant of H is zero, so H is singular and has no inverse.

Multiplying it out is also a check on part (a). || c: $\det H = (6)(3) - (9)(2) = 18 - 18 = 0$. The determinant of H is zero, so H is singular and has no inverse.

findTheMistake.stem: Daithí was asked to find $N^{-1}$, where $N = \begin{pmatrix}-3 & 2 \\ 4 & -1\end{pmatrix}$. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Lines 1 and 2 are both right: the determinant is correct, sign included, and the swapping and negating is exactly right. Line 1 carries the first of the two marks.
Line 3 writes the reciprocal as $\frac{1}{5}$, dropping the minus sign that line 1 had already found. The factor is $\frac{1}{-5}$.
Because the factor multiplies all four entries, one dropped sign makes every entry wrong: the answer should be $(1/5 2/5 ; 4/5 3/5)$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The determinant is right, sign included, so the first mark stands; the second is for the finished inverse, and line 3 is where it went. The fix is a pair of brackets: write the factor as one over the determinant in brackets, sign attached, straight after you work the determinant out. Then check by multiplying back — the identity will not appear if a sign is wrong.

findTheMistake.stem: Bríd was asked to find $R^{-1}$, where $R = \begin{pmatrix}4 & 9 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}$. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are right, the determinant's sign included. Line 3 writes the factor as $\frac{1}{1}$, dropping the minus sign that line 1 found. The factor is $\frac{1}{-1}$, which changes the sign of all four entries: $R^{-1} = \begin{pmatrix}-2 & 9 \\ 1 & -4\end{pmatrix}$.
findTheMistake.feedback: The determinant is right, sign and all, so the first mark stands; the finished inverse is where the second went. Keep the determinant in brackets inside the factor, and check by multiplying back: her matrix times R gives the identity with every sign turned over.

prompts.prompt: How is the determinant of a two by two matrix worked out?
prompts.answer: It is $ad - bc$: the leading diagonal multiplied, take away the other diagonal multiplied.

prompts.prompt: Give the three actions that turn a two by two matrix into its inverse.
prompts.answer: Swap the leading diagonal, change the signs on the other diagonal, and divide every entry by the determinant.

prompts.prompt: When does a matrix have no inverse, and what is it called?
prompts.answer: When its determinant is zero, because the formula divides by the determinant. Such a matrix is called singular.

prompts.prompt: A determinant comes out as $-5$. What is the factor in front of the swapped and negated matrix?
prompts.answer: $\frac{1}{-5}$, with the minus sign kept. Writing $\frac{1}{5}$ changes the sign of all four entries.

prompts.prompt: How do you check an inverse you have just written down?
prompts.answer: Multiply it by the original matrix. The answer should be the identity, with ones on the leading diagonal and zeros elsewhere.

prompts.prompt: What does the Unit 1 formula sheet give you about matrices?
prompts.answer: Nothing. The determinant and the inverse formula are both recall, which is why they are worth holding as a picture of three actions.

prompts.prompt: A question asks why an equation involving a matrix cannot be solved. What two things does the answer need?
prompts.answer: That the determinant is zero, and the name of the matrix whose determinant it is: for example, B has no inverse because det B = 0.

prompts.prompt: A determinant is negative. What sign has the factor in front of the inverse?
prompts.answer: Negative: one over the determinant, sign kept.
